prompt: Match each type of rock to how it forms.

right.text: Molten rock (magma or lava) cools and hardens
Layers of sediment are compacted and cemented
Existing rock is changed by heat and pressure

hints: *Meta* means change, and *morph* means shape or form.
solution: Igneous: cooled molten rock. Sedimentary: compacted and cemented layers of sediment. Metamorphic: rock changed by heat and pressure without melting.

prompt: Which layer of the Earth is the **thinnest**?

options.text: Crust
Mantle
Outer core
Inner core

feedback.b: The mantle is the thickest layer, about 2900 km.
feedback.c: The outer core is about 2200 km thick.
feedback.d: The inner core is over 1000 km in radius.

hints: One layer is only tens of kilometres thick. The others are thousands of kilometres thick.
solution: The **crust** is only about 5–50 km thick, very thin compared with the whole Earth, whose radius is about 6400 km. It's like the skin on an apple.

prompt: What is molten rock called once it has come out onto Earth's surface?
hints: Underground it is called magma.
solution: **Lava.** Molten rock underground is magma; when it erupts onto the surface it is called lava.

prompt: From the outside in, Earth's layers are the crust, the [[a]], the outer core and the [[b]].
hints: The thickest layer lies just under the crust.
solution: Crust → **mantle** → outer core → **inner core**.

prompt: Which rock is most likely to contain **fossils**?

options.text: Limestone
Granite
Basalt
Marble

feedback.b: Granite is igneous. It formed from molten rock, which would destroy any remains of living things.
feedback.c: Basalt is igneous. It formed from lava, so fossils are very unlikely.
feedback.d: Marble is metamorphic. The heat and pressure that formed it usually destroy fossils.

hints: Fossils form when remains are buried in layers of sediment.
solution: **Limestone** is a sedimentary rock, often made from the shells and skeletons of sea creatures, so it often contains fossils. Igneous rocks formed from molten rock, and metamorphic rocks were changed by heat and pressure, so fossils rarely survive in them.

prompt: What is the difference between **weathering** and **erosion**?

options.text: Weathering breaks rock down; erosion moves the pieces away
Weathering moves rock; erosion breaks it down
They are two words for the same thing
Weathering only happens in cold places; erosion only happens in hot places

feedback.c: They are linked, but they are different processes.
feedback.d: Both happen everywhere, though freeze–thaw weathering needs freezing temperatures.

hints: A rock can be broken up while it stays in the same place.
solution: **Weathering** breaks rock into smaller pieces where it is. **Erosion** moves those pieces away, carried by water, wind, ice or gravity.

prompt: New Zealand sits on the boundary between the Pacific Plate and the [[a]] Plate.
hints: This plate lies to the west of New Zealand, under the Tasman Sea.
solution: New Zealand sits on the boundary between the Pacific Plate and the **Australian** Plate. Their movement causes our earthquakes and volcanoes.

prompt: Which of these can **erode** rock (carry broken pieces away)? Select **all** that apply.

options.text: Rivers
Wind
Glaciers
Gravity (landslides)
Magma
Moonlight

hints: Erosion needs something that can pick up and move pieces of rock.
solution: **Rivers, wind, glaciers and gravity** (as well as waves) all move weathered rock. Magma is molten rock underground, and moonlight can't move anything.

prompt: Which metamorphic rock forms when **limestone** is heated and squeezed deep underground?
hints: It's often polished and used for statues and kitchen benches.
solution: **Marble.** Tākaka Hill, near Nelson, is made of marble.

prompt: What is the name for a crack in Earth's crust where blocks of rock move past each other?
hints: Earthquakes happen when rocks suddenly slip along one of these.
solution: A **fault**. When stress builds up along a fault and the rocks suddenly slip, we feel an earthquake.

prompt: Which layer of the Earth is made of **liquid** iron and nickel?
hints: The core has two parts, and only one of them is liquid.
solution: The **outer core** is liquid iron and nickel. The inner core is also iron and nickel, but it is solid because of the huge pressure.

prompt: Select **all** the things that make up soil.

options.text: Small particles of weathered rock
Humus (decayed plant and animal material)
Water
Air
Magma
Liquid iron

hints: Soil forms at the surface from rock and once-living material.
Worms and plant roots need something to breathe in the soil.
solution: Soil is a mixture of **weathered rock particles**, **humus**, **water** and **air**, plus living things such as worms, fungi and bacteria. Magma and liquid iron are found deep inside the Earth.

prompt: Granite has large crystals that you can see easily. What does this tell you about how it formed?

options.text: Magma cooled slowly deep underground, giving the crystals time to grow
Lava cooled quickly at the surface
Layers of sand were squashed together
It was squeezed so hard that its crystals grew

feedback.b: Quick cooling at the surface gives tiny crystals, as in basalt.
feedback.c: That describes a sedimentary rock such as sandstone, which is made of grains, not crystals that grew from molten rock.
feedback.d: Granite is igneous: it formed from molten rock, not by squeezing.

hints: Crystals grow while molten rock is cooling. More time means bigger crystals.
solution: Large crystals mean the magma **cooled slowly**, which happens deep underground, where the surrounding rock keeps it insulated. The crystals had plenty of time to grow. Granite is an igneous rock.

prompt: Put the stages of fossil formation in order.

items.text: A sea creature dies and sinks to the sea floor
It is quickly buried by sediment, and its soft parts rot away
Over millions of years, minerals replace the hard parts, such as shell and bone
The rock is pushed up and eroded, exposing the fossil

hints: The organism has to be covered before it can be preserved.
The last step brings the fossil back to the surface.
solution: Dies → quickly buried (the soft parts rot away) → minerals replace the hard parts over millions of years → uplift and erosion expose the fossil.

prompt: How do the plates mainly move along the **Alpine Fault** in the South Island?

options.text: They slide past each other sideways
One plate sinks down beneath the other
They move apart, and new crust forms between them
They don't move at all

feedback.b: That's subduction, which happens under the North Island.
feedback.c: That happens at mid-ocean ridges, not in New Zealand.
feedback.d: The plates move a few centimetres each year, and that's why the fault produces large earthquakes.

hints: Rocks on either side of the fault have been shifted about 480 km along it.
solution: Along the Alpine Fault the Pacific and Australian Plates mainly **slide past each other sideways**. They are also squeezed together, which pushes up the Southern Alps.

prompt: Which statement about Earth's **mantle** is correct?

options.text: It is mostly solid rock that is hot enough to flow very slowly
It is a layer of liquid magma
It is the thinnest layer of the Earth
It is made of solid iron and nickel

feedback.b: This is a common mistake. The mantle is mostly solid. Magma forms only where rock melts, for example above a subducting plate.
feedback.c: The crust is the thinnest. The mantle is the thickest layer, about 2900 km.

hints: It behaves a bit like very thick toffee.
solution: The mantle is very hot rock that is **mostly solid but can flow very slowly**. Convection currents in the mantle help to move the tectonic plates.

prompt: Rocks at the surface are broken down by [[a]] and carried away by erosion. The sediment is deposited in layers, then compacted and cemented to form [[b]] rock. If this rock is buried deeply and heated and squeezed, it becomes [[c]] rock.
hints: The process that breaks rock in place comes before erosion.
Think about what the second rock is made from.
solution: **Weathering** breaks rock down; the sediment forms **sedimentary** rock; heat and pressure turn it into **metamorphic** rock.

prompt: Explain how **freeze–thaw** weathering breaks up rocks high in the Southern Alps.
modelAnswer: Rainwater or melted snow seeps into cracks in the rock. At night the water freezes and expands as it turns to ice, which pushes the crack wider. During the day the ice melts, and the water seeps further in. Freezing and thawing again and again widens the crack until pieces of rock break off.

rubric.criterion: Water gets into cracks and expands when it freezes, pushing the crack wider
Repeated freezing and thawing widens the crack until pieces break off

hints: What happens to the volume of water when it freezes?
Why does this happen many times in the mountains?
solution: Water in cracks expands as it freezes, levering the crack open. Repeated day–night freezing and thawing eventually splits pieces off. That's why there are piles of broken rock (scree) on mountain slopes.

prompt: Suppose the rocks on either side of the Alpine Fault move past each other by about 3 cm each year. How far would they move in 1000 years? Give your answer in **metres**.
hints: First find the distance in centimetres.
There are 100 cm in 1 m.
solution: $3 \times 1000 = 3000$ cm, and $3000 \div 100 = $ **30 m**. Over millions of years, small yearly movements add up to hundreds of kilometres.

prompt: Describe how a piece of sandstone (a sedimentary rock) could eventually become part of an igneous rock. Name the processes involved.
modelAnswer: The sandstone is buried deeper and deeper (for example as plates push together). The heat and pressure change it into a metamorphic rock (quartzite) without melting it. If it is carried deep enough to get even hotter, it melts and becomes magma. The magma then rises and cools and hardens, either underground or as lava at the surface, forming igneous rock.

rubric.criterion: Buried deeply, heat and pressure change it into metamorphic rock
At high enough temperatures the rock melts to form magma
The magma cools and hardens (crystallises) to form igneous rock

hints: What must happen to any rock before it can become igneous?
There's usually a stage in between, as it gets buried deeper.
solution: Burial → heat and pressure → metamorphic rock → melting → magma → cooling → igneous rock. (A sedimentary rock can also melt directly if it gets hot enough.)

prompt: A cliff shows three layers of sedimentary rock that have not been disturbed. The **bottom** layer contains fossil sea shells. The **middle** layer contains fossil leaves. The **top** layer contains no fossils. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The bottom layer is the oldest, and the area was once under the sea
The top layer is the oldest because it has been exposed the longest
All three layers formed at the same time
The area has always been dry land

feedback.b: Layers are laid down one on top of another, so the top layer is the youngest.
feedback.c: Sediment builds up layer by layer over long periods of time.
feedback.d: Fossil sea shells show that the area was once covered by the sea.

hints: Which layer had to be laid down first?
What do sea-shell fossils tell you about where that layer formed?
solution: In undisturbed layers, the **lowest is the oldest**, because each layer settles on top of the one before. Sea-shell fossils show that the bottom layer formed under the sea. The fossil leaves in the layer above suggest land plants grew nearby later.

prompt: Fossils of sea shells are found in rocks high up in some of New Zealand's mountain ranges. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The rocks formed under the sea and were later pushed up by plate movements
Birds carried the shells up the mountains
The sea used to cover the tops of the mountains as they are today
The shellfish lived on the mountains

feedback.b: Birds might move a few shells, but not whole layers of rock full of fossils.
feedback.c: The rocks have moved up; the sea hasn't risen thousands of metres.
feedback.d: These shells come from sea creatures, which can't live on land.

hints: Where do sea shells form? How could that rock end up high on a mountain?
solution: The shells were buried in sediment on the **sea floor**, which became sedimentary rock. Over millions of years, plate movements **pushed the rock up** to form mountains. This is how fossils give evidence of past environments and Earth's movements.

prompt: Which of these are mainly caused by the plates squeezing and sliding along the **Alpine Fault**? Select **all** that apply.

options.text: The Southern Alps being pushed up
Large earthquakes on the West Coast of the South Island
Rock layers and streams that have been shifted sideways along the fault
The volcanoes of the Taupō Volcanic Zone
The geysers at Rotorua

hints: The Alpine Fault is in the South Island.
What causes the volcanoes and geysers of the central North Island?
solution: Along the Alpine Fault, squeezing pushes up the **Southern Alps**, sudden slips cause **large earthquakes**, and sideways movement **shifts rocks and streams**. The Taupō volcanoes and Rotorua's geysers come from subduction under the North Island.

prompt: The plate boundary behaves differently under the North Island and the South Island. Compare the two, and explain why the North Island has active volcanoes but the South Island does not.
modelAnswer: Under the North Island, the Pacific Plate is subducting (sliding down) beneath the Australian Plate. As it goes deep into the hot mantle, rock melts to form magma, which rises and feeds the volcanoes of the Taupō Volcanic Zone. In the South Island, the plates mainly slide past each other along the Alpine Fault, and are squeezed together, pushing up the Southern Alps. There is no subduction along the Alpine Fault, so no magma forms under the South Island. It has large earthquakes but no active volcanoes.

rubric.criterion: North Island: the Pacific Plate subducts beneath the Australian Plate
Subduction carries rock deep into the hot mantle, where melting makes magma that rises to form volcanoes (Taupō Volcanic Zone)
South Island: the plates slide past each other (and push together) along the Alpine Fault
No subduction along the Alpine Fault, so no magma forms under the South Island: earthquakes and mountains, but no active volcanoes

hints: What does one plate do under the North Island?
Volcanoes need magma. Where does magma come from?
solution: North Island: subduction → melting → magma → volcanoes. South Island: sideways sliding and squeezing along the Alpine Fault → earthquakes and the Southern Alps, but no magma, so no active volcanoes.

prompt: Limestone areas such as Waitomo have many caves, but granite areas have very few. Which explanation is best?

options.text: Rainwater is slightly acidic, so it slowly dissolves limestone (calcium carbonate), but it barely affects granite
Limestone is much softer, so rivers wear caves straight through it
Granite is too hot underground for caves to form
Caves form only in igneous rocks, and limestone is igneous

feedback.b: Rivers do some of the work, but the key process is chemical: acidic water dissolves the limestone.
feedback.c: Granite near the surface is not hot. The difference is how the rocks react with water.
feedback.d: Limestone is sedimentary, and caves like Waitomo are not formed in igneous rock.

hints: Rain absorbs some carbon dioxide from the air. What does that make it?
Limestone is calcium carbonate. What happens when an acid meets a carbonate?
solution: Rain dissolves a little carbon dioxide from the air, so it is **slightly acidic**. Limestone is calcium carbonate, which reacts with acids, so over a very long time the water **dissolves** channels and caves through it. This is chemical weathering. Granite doesn't react with weak acid in the same way.

prompt: Which arrow shows **melting**?

options.text: P
Q
S
T

feedback.p: P goes from magma to igneous rock. That is the opposite of melting: the molten rock cools and hardens.
feedback.q: Q breaks igneous rock down into sediment. That is weathering and erosion, not melting.
feedback.s: S turns sedimentary rock into metamorphic rock by heat and pressure, but without melting it.

hints: Melting makes molten rock. Which arrow points to magma?
solution: **T**: metamorphic rock heated enough to melt becomes magma.

prompt: Match each arrow to the process it shows.
hints: Sediment is made of small broken pieces of rock.
Sedimentary rock forms when layers of sediment are squashed and stuck together.
solution: P: magma **cools and crystallises** into igneous rock. Q: rock is broken down and carried away by **weathering and erosion**. R: sediment is **compacted and cemented** into sedimentary rock. S: **heat and pressure** change it into metamorphic rock.

prompt: Mt Taranaki is made of igneous rock that formed from lava. Describe how some of this rock could eventually become part of a **sedimentary** rock. Name the processes involved.
modelAnswer: First the rock on the mountain is broken into small pieces by weathering, for example by freeze–thaw or by rainwater. Then the pieces are carried away by erosion, for example by rivers, down to the sea, where they are deposited in layers on the sea floor. Over a long time the layers are buried under more sediment, squashed (compacted) and stuck together (cemented) by minerals, forming sedimentary rock.

rubric.criterion: Weathering breaks the igneous rock into small pieces (sediment)
Erosion carries the sediment away (e.g. by rivers) and it is deposited in layers
The layers are buried, compacted and cemented to form sedimentary rock

hints: Follow arrows Q and R on the diagram.
Name the process for each stage: breaking down, moving, and turning back into rock.
solution: Weathering → erosion and deposition in layers → burial, compaction and cementation → sedimentary rock.

stem: The Alpine Fault runs for about 600 km along the western side of the Southern Alps. It is part of the boundary between the Australian Plate and the Pacific Plate. Geologists have found evidence that it has produced a large earthquake roughly every 300 years. The last one was in 1717.
prompt: In 2017, scientists marked an anniversary of the last large Alpine Fault earthquake. How many years had passed since that earthquake?
hints: Subtract 1717 from 2017.
solution: 2017 − 1717 = **300 years**, the same as the average gap between large earthquakes. Every year since then has taken it further past that average.

stem: The Alpine Fault runs for about 600 km along the western side of the Southern Alps. It is part of the boundary between the Australian Plate and the Pacific Plate. Geologists have found evidence that it has produced a large earthquake roughly every 300 years. The last one was in 1717.
prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the evidence?

options.text: A large Alpine Fault earthquake is likely in the coming decades, but nobody can predict exactly when
The next large earthquake will happen exactly 300 years after 1717
There will be no more large earthquakes, because the 1717 earthquake released all the stress
Earthquakes only happen every 300 years, so the area is completely safe until then

feedback.b: "Roughly every 300 years" is an average. The gaps between past earthquakes have varied, so an exact date can't be predicted. Also, 1717 + 300 = 2017, which has already passed.
feedback.c: The plates are still moving, so stress keeps building up again after each earthquake.
feedback.d: The 300 years is only an average, and smaller earthquakes can happen at any time.

hints: "Roughly every 300 years" is an average. Can an average give an exact date?
solution: More than 300 years have passed since 1717, which is longer than the average gap, so a large earthquake is **likely in the coming decades**. But the gaps vary, so scientists cannot say exactly when. This is why people on the West Coast prepare for it now.

stem: The Alpine Fault runs for about 600 km along the western side of the Southern Alps. It is part of the boundary between the Australian Plate and the Pacific Plate. Geologists have found evidence that it has produced a large earthquake roughly every 300 years. The last one was in 1717.
prompt: The plates on either side of the Alpine Fault move past each other by a few centimetres every year. Explain how this slow movement leads to **large, sudden** earthquakes.
modelAnswer: The plates keep moving past each other, but friction makes the rocks on either side of the fault stick together (lock). As the plates keep moving, the rocks bend and stress builds up over hundreds of years. When the stress becomes greater than the friction holding the rocks, they suddenly slip, moving several metres in seconds. The stored energy is released as shaking (seismic waves), which is the earthquake.

rubric.criterion: Friction makes the rocks along the fault stick or lock, even though the plates keep moving
Stress (energy) builds up in the rocks over a long time as they bend
When the stress is too great, the rocks suddenly slip, releasing the energy as shaking (an earthquake)

hints: Why don't the rocks slide smoothly past each other all the time?
What builds up while the rocks are stuck?
solution: Rocks lock because of friction → stress builds up for centuries → sudden slip releases the energy as an earthquake.

prompt: Which of these rocks formed from **lava** that cooled at Earth's surface? Select **all** that apply.

options.text: Granite
Basalt
Pumice
Obsidian

hints: Rock that cools at the surface cools quickly, so its crystals are small or missing.
solution: **Basalt, pumice and obsidian** cooled quickly from lava at the surface, so they have tiny crystals or none. Granite has large crystals because it cooled slowly from magma deep underground.

prompt: Put these three rocks in order of how quickly they cooled, from **fastest** to **slowest**.
hints: The slower molten rock cools, the more time crystals have to grow.
solution: Crystal size shows the cooling speed. **Obsidian** (no crystals) cooled fastest, then **basalt** (very small crystals), then **granite** (large crystals), which cooled slowest, deep underground.

prompt: Explain how pumice forms, and why it can float on water.
modelAnswer: Pumice forms when magma containing a lot of dissolved gas erupts explosively. As the pressure drops, the gas forms bubbles, making a froth, and the frothy lava cools so quickly that the bubbles are trapped as the rock hardens. This leaves pumice full of holes. Because so much of its volume is gas-filled holes, its overall density is less than the density of water, so it floats.

rubric.criterion: Gas-rich magma or lava erupts and froths up with gas bubbles
It cools very quickly, so the gas bubbles are trapped as holes in the rock
The holes make its overall density less than water, so it floats

hints: Where did the bubbles come from, and why didn't they escape?
Compare the density of pumice with the density of water.
solution: Frothy, gas-rich lava cools fast and traps bubbles → lots of holes → overall less dense than water → floats.

prompt: What is the name for the remains or traces of an ancient living thing preserved in rock?
hints: Dinosaur bones and shell prints in rocks are examples.
solution: They are **fossils**. Footprints and burrows preserved in rock count as fossils too.

prompt: Earth's crust and the top of the mantle are broken into huge, slowly moving pieces. What are these pieces called?
hints: New Zealand sits across the boundary between two of them.
solution: They are **tectonic plates**. New Zealand sits across the boundary between the Australian Plate and the Pacific Plate.

prompt: Which of these rocks is **sedimentary**?

options.text: Sandstone
Granite
Basalt
Marble

feedback.b: Granite is igneous: it formed from magma that cooled slowly underground.
feedback.c: Basalt is igneous: it formed from lava that cooled quickly.
feedback.d: Marble is metamorphic: it formed when limestone was heated and squeezed.

hints: Sedimentary rocks are made from grains of sediment, such as sand, stuck together.
solution: **Sandstone** is sedimentary: grains of sand were deposited in layers, then compacted and cemented together.

prompt: Select **all** the examples of **weathering** (breaking rock down where it is), not erosion.

options.text: Water freezing in a crack and splitting the rock
Tree roots growing into a crack and forcing it apart
Slightly acidic rainwater slowly dissolving limestone
A river carrying pebbles downstream
Wind blowing sand along a beach
A glacier dragging rocks down a valley

hints: Weathering breaks rock down. Erosion moves the pieces somewhere else.
solution: **Freeze–thaw, tree roots and acid rain** all break rock down where it is: physical, biological and chemical weathering. Rivers, wind and glaciers **move** rock, which is erosion.

prompt: Which layer of a soil usually contains the most **humus** (decayed plant and animal material)?

options.text: Topsoil
Subsoil
Bedrock
All layers have the same amount

feedback.b: Subsoil is below the topsoil. It has less humus and is usually lighter in colour.
feedback.c: Bedrock is the solid rock underneath the soil. It contains no humus.
feedback.d: Dead leaves and roots rot mainly near the surface, so humus is concentrated at the top.

hints: Where do dead leaves fall and rot?
solution: The **topsoil** has the most humus, because dead plants and animals decay at the surface. That is why topsoil is usually the darkest layer and the best for growing plants.

prompt: Put the stages of soil formation on bare rock in order.

items.text: Bare rock is weathered into small fragments
Lichens and mosses start to grow on the fragments
Dead lichens and mosses decay, adding humus
Larger plants grow, and their roots break up the rock further and the soil gets deeper

hints: Plants need some small particles to grow in before they can add humus.
solution: Weathering makes small fragments → simple plants such as lichens and mosses grow → they die and decay into humus → larger plants grow, their roots break the rock further, and the soil deepens. This takes hundreds to thousands of years.

prompt: Otago schist has thin, shiny, flaky layers. It formed when greywacke (a hard sedimentary rock) was buried deep underground and was heated and squeezed, but did **not** melt. What type of rock is schist?

options.text: Metamorphic
Sedimentary, because it has layers
Igneous, because it was heated
It is still greywacke, so it is sedimentary

feedback.b: Metamorphic rocks can have layers too. Schist's layers formed from squeezing, not from sediment being deposited.
feedback.c: Igneous rocks form when molten rock cools. Schist was heated but never melted.
feedback.d: Heat and pressure changed the minerals and texture, so it has become a new rock.

hints: Which type of rock forms when existing rock is changed by heat and pressure, without melting?
solution: Schist is **metamorphic**: existing rock (greywacke) was changed by heat and pressure deep underground without melting. Its shiny layers are new minerals lined up by the squeezing.

prompt: What is thought to drive the slow movement of the tectonic plates?

options.text: Convection currents in the hot, slowly flowing rock of the mantle
The pull of the Moon's gravity, the same force that causes tides
Earthquakes pushing the plates along
Liquid iron in the outer core pushing directly on the crust

feedback.b: The Moon causes tides in the sea, but it is not what moves the plates.
feedback.c: Earthquakes are caused by the plates moving, not the other way round.
feedback.d: The outer core is thousands of kilometres below the crust, with the whole mantle in between.

hints: Heat from deep inside the Earth makes the mantle rock flow very slowly in loops.
solution: Heat from inside the Earth makes the mantle rock flow very slowly in **convection currents**: hot rock rises, spreads out, cools and sinks. The plates on top are carried along, a few centimetres a year.

prompt: Lake Taupō fills a [[a]], a huge hollow that formed when the ground [[b]] into the partly emptied magma chamber after enormous volcanic eruptions.
hints: After a huge eruption, the magma underground has gone. What happens to the ground above it?
solution: Lake Taupō fills a **caldera**. After enormous eruptions emptied much of the magma chamber, the ground above **collapsed** into it, leaving a huge basin that filled with water. A crater is much smaller and is blasted out by an eruption.

prompt: Describe how igneous rocks and sedimentary rocks form, and give **one** feature you could look for to tell them apart.
modelAnswer: Igneous rocks form when molten rock (magma underground or lava at the surface) cools and hardens. Sedimentary rocks form when layers of sediment, such as sand, mud or shells, are deposited, buried, compacted and cemented together. To tell them apart: igneous rocks are made of interlocking crystals and never contain fossils, while sedimentary rocks are often in layers, are made of grains stuck together, and may contain fossils.

rubric.criterion: Igneous: molten rock cools and hardens; sedimentary: layers of sediment compacted and cemented
One distinguishing feature, e.g. igneous has interlocking crystals and no fossils; sedimentary has layers, grains or fossils

hints: One type starts as molten rock; the other starts as broken bits of rock.
Which type could contain a fossil shell?
solution: Igneous: cooled molten rock with interlocking crystals. Sedimentary: compacted and cemented sediment, often layered, sometimes with fossils.

prompt: Suppose a tectonic plate moves 5 cm every year. How far would it move in 1 million years? Give your answer in **kilometres**.
hints: First find the distance in centimetres.
100 cm = 1 m and 1000 m = 1 km.
solution: 5 cm × 1,000,000 = 5,000,000 cm = 50,000 m = **50 km**. Tiny yearly movements add up to huge distances over geological time.

prompt: Earth's inner core is even hotter than its outer core, yet the inner core is **solid** while the outer core is liquid. Why?

options.text: The enormous pressure at the centre of the Earth keeps the iron and nickel solid
The inner core is made of rock, which has a higher melting point than metal
The inner core is actually cooler, because heat rises away from it
The inner core is frozen because no heat can reach the centre of the Earth

feedback.b: Both the inner and outer core are made mostly of iron and nickel.
feedback.c: The inner core is the hottest part of the Earth, at about 5400 °C.
feedback.d: The centre is the hottest part of the Earth, not a frozen one.

hints: Think about the weight of everything pressing down on the centre of the Earth.
solution: The weight of all the rock and metal above creates **enormous pressure** at the centre. This squeezes the iron and nickel so hard that they stay solid, even at about 5400 °C.

prompt: During the 2016 Kaikōura earthquake, parts of the rocky shore were suddenly lifted up by several metres, leaving seaweed and pāua stranded high and dry. What does this show?

options.text: Plate movements can suddenly raise land, and many such movements over time can lift sea-floor rocks into mountains
The sea level suddenly dropped all around New Zealand
The tide went out much further than usual that day
The seaweed and pāua moved up the shore to escape the shaking

feedback.b: The sea level didn't change. The land itself moved up, and only along parts of the coast.
feedback.c: The tide comes back in a few hours later. This shore stayed high and dry permanently.
feedback.d: Seaweed is attached to the rocks and can't move, and pāua can't climb several metres in seconds.

hints: Was it the water or the land that moved?
solution: The **land was pushed up** by the plate movement during the earthquake. Repeated uplift like this, over millions of years, is how rocks that formed under the sea (with fossil shells) end up high in New Zealand's mountains.

prompt: A distinctive belt of unusual rock is found near Nelson. An identical belt of the same rock is found in Otago and Southland, about 480 km away, on the other side of the Alpine Fault. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The two belts formed together as one belt and have been moved apart along the Alpine Fault over millions of years
The same unusual rock happened to form in two separate places by coincidence
A river carried a huge amount of the rock 480 km from Nelson to Southland
One very large earthquake moved the rocks 480 km apart in a few minutes

feedback.b: Very unlikely: the two belts match closely in rock type and age, and each ends right at the fault, which points to one belt that has been split.
feedback.c: Rivers carry sediment, not whole belts of solid bedrock, and they don't flow across mountain ranges.
feedback.d: A single large earthquake moves rocks a few metres. Hundreds of kilometres takes millions of years of movement.

hints: How do the plates move along the Alpine Fault?
How far could a few centimetres a year add up to over millions of years?
solution: The two belts were once joined. The plates have slid sideways past each other along the Alpine Fault, a few centimetres a year and several metres in each big earthquake, which over millions of years has moved the two halves about **480 km apart**. This is strong evidence for plate movement.

prompt: In a swamp in the central North Island, scientists dig down through undisturbed layers of mud. They find a layer of ash from the Taupō eruption of about 1800 years ago. Moa bones are found in the mud **below** the ash layer. What can they conclude?

options.text: The moa died more than about 1800 years ago
The moa died less than about 1800 years ago
The moa died during the Taupō eruption
Nothing, because the ash tells us nothing about the mud below it

feedback.b: In undisturbed layers, deeper layers are older. Mud below the ash was laid down before the ash fell.
feedback.c: The bones are in the mud below the ash, so they were already there before the ash fell. Being near the ash doesn't mean they died at the same time.
feedback.d: The ash layer has a known age, so it tells us that everything below it is older.

hints: In undisturbed layers, which are older: the ones at the bottom or the ones on top?
solution: In undisturbed layers, lower layers are **older**. The mud with the bones was laid down before the ash fell, so the moa died **more than about 1800 years ago**. A layer of known age like this ash helps scientists date the layers around it.

prompt: Discuss how the rock cycle is driven by **two** sources of energy: energy from the Sun, and heat from inside the Earth. Give examples of processes powered by each.
modelAnswer: Energy from the Sun drives the weather and the water cycle. This powers weathering and erosion: for example, rain, freeze–thaw and wind break rocks down, and rivers and wind carry the sediment away until it is deposited, where it can form sedimentary rock. Heat from inside the Earth drives the processes that happen deep underground. It melts rock to make magma, which cools to form igneous rock, and together with pressure it changes rocks into metamorphic rock. Earth's internal heat also drives convection in the mantle, which moves the plates, pushing up mountains so that rocks are exposed to weathering again and burying other rocks deep down.

rubric.criterion: The Sun drives the weather and water cycle, which cause weathering
The Sun drives erosion and deposition of sediment (e.g. rivers, wind), leading to sedimentary rock
Earth's internal heat causes melting (magma and igneous rock) and metamorphism
Earth's internal heat drives plate movement, which uplifts rocks to the surface or buries them, linking the two halves of the cycle

hints: Which processes happen at the surface, and which deep underground?
What lifts buried rock back up to the surface?
solution: Sun: weather and water cycle → weathering, erosion, deposition. Internal heat: melting, metamorphism and plate movement (uplift and burial). Together they keep rock moving around the cycle.
